items.question: How do you judge the promises being made about turning robots into productive employees?
items.object: Robot commercialization promises and the industry's credibility
items.answer: I think we should stop doing things that tarnish our industry's reputation—for example, promising people that if they collect data, they can train it, or that if they build a factory, they will have skills; selling robots and saying, “You collect it, you train it—tomorrow it will be your employee.” These models are frightening. They are smashing this industry's rice bowl. That is the first thing: demonstrate publicly, and do not allow asking for data. Some people in China are very bold now: they dare not tell others they are asking for data, but in fact they are. If, within five years, we still cannot form productivity at the scale of tens of thousands of units, then our field will have been falsified.

items.question: How do you understand the recent surge of interest in embodied intelligence from your experience entering the field?
items.object: The recent surge of interest in embodied intelligence
items.answer:
I can only say that people have begun to recognize practitioners in this field. From my perspective—having entered robotics mainly through 3D vision after beginning work in AI—it really went through an initially slow warm-up. Then, in the United States, after 2021—actually, one should say 2020—embodied intelligence had already become a very mainstream research direction among young scholars.

So in 2021, when I returned to Peking University—essentially, I got the Peking University offer at the end of 2020—I was basically all in on embodied AI. We named our lab the Embodied Perception and Interaction Lab. This was, as far as I know, the first lab in mainland China to name itself after embodiment. When I returned to China in 2021, virtually no one was doing it. At that time, you could not even find the term “embodied intelligence” by searching for it.

items.question: Why did you think embodied intelligence needed to be developed immediately?
items.object: The case for developing embodied intelligence
items.answer: Our core line of thought was that intelligence in the digital domain essentially mines knowledge from existing data such as the internet, and then drives intelligence in a virtual, digital environment without physical entities. But intelligence in the physical world necessarily needs a body. This part is not on the internet's current data; it requires physical interaction in the real world. Put plainly, every application involving hands-on work needs this kind of intelligence and this kind of data, so we should begin doing it immediately.

items.question: What do you see as the core distinction between internet AI and embodied AI?
items.object: The distinction between internet AI and embodied AI
items.answer:
In 2020, I remember very clearly that online, in U.S. academic circles, people had begun to stop calling it embodied agent. Because agent, as we see it today, is very oriented toward bots that automatically do work in the digital world. To distinguish it, in the physical world we used the word robot directly. Then, in 2020, slides began appearing online that discussed internet AI versus embodied AI. This was in U.S. academic circles.

The core distinction was that internet AI gets its data and knowledge from the internet, while embodied AI comes from interaction between the body and the environment—acting in person. It is either data created through interaction with an environment in a simulator, following that simulator's laws of physics, or all sorts of data created through real-world interaction, producing intelligence. So by 2020, the term was gradually taking shape in the United States.

items.question: How do you understand the emphasis behind calling the field embodied intelligence rather than robotics?
items.object: The term “embodied intelligence” and its roots in computer vision
items.answer:
It relates to the field from which embodied intelligence emerged. We see that in the United States, the field was mainly driven by scholars in computer vision. That is why people talked about internet AI versus embodied AI.

Because in computer vision, from ImageNet and facial recognition to semantic segmentation, these things all relied on human-labeled data from the internet. After everyone in the field competed and competed until they felt, “Ah, this paradigm is settled; everything afterward is an engineering problem,” they began to ask what came next. Someone proposed using vision to empower robots. From computer vision's perspective, this meant moving from the digital world into the physical world, while still being vision-based intelligence.

That is why, from the computer-vision perspective, they would say: what I am doing now is internet AI, okay; next comes embodied AI. It is not at all about comparing it with robotics or calling what computer vision does robotics. It means: you can regard what I do now as digital vision; next I will do robotic vision.

items.question: How do you understand robotics as a field that spans several academic disciplines?
items.object: Robotics as a discipline spanning mechanical engineering, computer science, and electrical engineering
items.answer: I would say mechanical engineering and control are basically the traditional strongholds of robotics. Mechanical engineering is mainly responsible for designing the overall mechanical system. Naturally it involves the mechanical system from hardware through control. There are robotics directions in both CS and EE. Taking Stanford as an example, both computer science and electrical engineering have robotics-oriented directions, but their emphases differ. In CS there are many traditional search-based robotics algorithms, such as path planning. In EE, robotics also includes signal-based filtering methods, as well as how embedded systems support the robot's entire system based on its underlying electronic and electrical architecture. But historically, robotics is truly an all-encompassing thing. There is a saying that robotics has no independent scientific question of its own: it puts things from every discipline into itself. So Stanford has no robotics department.

items.question: How do you understand the historical focus of traditional robotics in relation to where robots were actually deployed?
items.object: Traditional robotics and its relationship to deployment scenarios
items.answer: Historically, the main body of robotics was about how to do control, how to design good hardware, and then complete it by combining it with control. That is also closely connected to the scenarios in which robots have mainly been deployed over the past decades. Let me give a few examples, such as industrial robots. Their mechanics are built so that their repeatability is very high. At the same time, repeatability is not just a pure hardware issue; the full set of control algorithms must also be very stable, avoiding points of control instability and so on. These are highly control-oriented and mathematical matters. For example, using a large robotic arm on a space station to do things—these are matters people in traditional robotics cared about greatly. Slightly more cutting-edge things, like nanorobots or robot fish, are relatively research-oriented things in robotics, the sort of work published in Nature or Science. But when we talk about large-scale application of robots, it is industrial robots.

items.question: Why do you think robotics researchers using reinforcement learning for control did not regard their work as embodied intelligence?
items.object: Reinforcement learning for robot control and the label of embodied intelligence
items.answer: What is done today is not to say that previous people did not do it at all. In control, some people also used reinforcement learning for control. For example, the University of Tokyo in Japan and ETH both had work using reinforcement learning for quadruped robots. But these works were, to a certain extent, data-driven, or hybrid control combining data-driven methods and traditional MPC in some way. Yet they did not call it embodied intelligence. In their view, using neural networks for control, using traditional mathematical modeling for control, or using simpler PID control are all control. Their control signals are things like joint angles—the variables supplied by joint encoders—and sensor signals, such as IMUs. Whether they were doing MPC before or reinforcement learning later, they did not actually feel that this had made anything fundamentally different.

items.question: What do you see as the conceptual shift that led computer-vision researchers to propose embodied AI?
items.object: Computer vision's conception of embodied AI
items.answer: It was in computer vision that people said vision needed to become active. That is, I do not passively receive images from the internet and have you ask me whether this is a cat or dog for me to classify; it is not that you give me a face and I say whether it belongs to this person or that person. Rather, I have the ability to observe actively, and the ability to interact with and affect the environment. items.question: How do you view the idea that language is the essence of intelligence?
items.object: Language as the essence of intelligence
items.answer: I do not really agree with that, because many organisms have intelligence but do not necessarily have language. Even little bugs that people think have no intelligence can fly all around. You cannot easily swat them, right? And many things with low-level intelligence forage for food and avoid natural enemies. Their ability to control their bodies and navigate may not even have been reached by today's VRA, yet you cannot say they lack intelligence. Vision is intelligence too—visual intelligence. It is just that if it is purely visual intelligence, its interpretability is poorer; it is end-to-end. That is to say, when ordinary organisms cannot speak, they are a pure VA model, not VRA. They cannot explain what they are doing, and they cannot communicate with others through the one-dimensional sequential data of language at an abstract level. So humans are very—we have very high intelligence. We compressed our communication into one-dimensional speech, thereby creating a more efficient, lower-dimensional mode of communication that everyone can somehow recognize. But it is not the essence of intelligence; indeed, it is a kind of intelligence that evolved only with extremely advanced intelligence.

items.question: How do you understand the role of the perception-action loop in computer vision’s transition to embodied AI?
items.object: The perception-action loop in computer vision’s transition to embodied AI
items.answer:
One example here is an early task through which embodied AI first arose: navigation. I give you a simulated environment that you have never seen. It differs from traditional SLAM techniques: it does not see a map and does not have a prebuilt map. A small wheeled robot or a little dog might be told, “Please find, for example, a chair for me.” This is called object-goal navigation.

At the time, computer vision quickly formed some consensus on why this was a very good first embodied, visual task. First, it interacts with the world. When I take one step, my coordinates in the world change. That action changes what the camera on my head sees. This is a very important behavioral pattern in human embodiment, called the perception-action loop. I first decide through perception what action to take. After I take an action, the environment changes. The simplest change is that the environment itself has not changed, but my position has changed, updating my perception signal. Then I can further take action.

Essentially, in the internet-AI era, the vision community realized that we only had perception and no action. If we take action, the environment must change and update my perception. Otherwise, say you give me a picture and I tell you it is a cat—there is nothing afterward. There is no longer any feedback from the environment about my recognition that it is a cat, nor any way to update the question and visual input. With internet AI, classification ends everything. items.question: Which events do you see as establishing embodied AI as an important field?

items.question: Why do you think early neural-network-based robotic grasping did not feel like an exciting departure from computer vision?
items.object: Early neural-network-based robotic grasping
items.answer: Around 2017, everyone had recognized that combining robotics and AI was a good approach, but exactly what problem it should solve—and what would make a real difference—was something everyone was exploring. There was already quite a bit of work on grasping, using neural networks, computer vision, and point clouds. items.question: How do you understand navigation's role in establishing the mainstream direction of embodied intelligence?
items.object: Navigation's role in the development of embodied intelligence
items.answer: I think the important thing was that people realized the perception-action loop was very important. Navigation strongly embodies the changing perspective—changing scenery with every step—and one must perceive again. Sometimes the tasks were even solvable by traditional methods, such as giving you a coordinate and telling you to go there in an environment, called point-goal navigation. Then the next, slightly harder task was object-goal navigation: give you a word and ask you to find it. These could also be handled with traditional or non-closed-loop methods in a modular way. But people did not insist on such modular methods; they wanted to explore around a closed-loop perception-action loop. Thus people such as Fei-Fei Li, Meta, and Jitendra Malik came forward to create, for example, Facebook's challenge—Habitat. They built a large simulator, a navigation simulator, and iterated step by step on it as task difficulty rose continuously. Navigation then became embodied intelligence's first task. Everyone first did research around this, thoroughly making perception and action a closed-loop model. Later they naturally went back to manipulation too: how to do closed-loop manipulation. Now navigation and manipulation are done together, and then large models open up tasks—you can name any task and it can do it. That gradually formed the most mainstream direction of embodied intelligence today.

items.question: How do you understand the problem that Deepak's curiosity-driven exploration work addressed in reinforcement learning?
items.object: Curiosity-driven exploration in reinforcement learning
items.answer: Let me give an example: how can you clear a Mario game? With reinforcement learning, you need rewards, and that is too hard unless you write an especially complex reward. If rewards are sparse—basically, only when you clear the level and the flag rises do you get a one; along the way, dying is negative one and there are no other rewards—with this kind of setup, reinforcement learning simply cannot explore its way to that final one. You must play for several minutes before you can discover the reward of one, while everything in between is zero; you cannot learn it. So at the time, they proposed an intrinsic reward function based on curiosity, allowing Mario to continually explore places he did not expect, places with large prediction errors relative to his own predictions.

items.question: How did you approach demonstrating multi-step human–object interaction in your 2016 project when you had no robotic arm?

items.question: How do you see your early research on learning human–object interactions from videos in relation to internet AI?
items.object: The relationship between early video-based human–object interaction research and internet AI
items.answer: Actually, I would not call it fully internet AI. As for the data, this data was hard to collect on the internet at the time. We filmed it ourselves. We sent people to make videos of tabletop-object manipulation and labeled what action occurred from which frame to which frame. Then we used an LSTM to learn causality between actions: what came first and what came afterward; how an action changed an object's state; how it made an object—for example, an empty bottle—unable to pour water for someone, whereas once it was full, it could. What we learned with the LSTM was essentially modeling the actions humans took, how the state of the environment changed, and, after it changed, what further actions humans were allowed to take—the causal relationships. That is exactly—the perception-action loop.

items.question: How did you approach demonstrating a model learned from human videos when you had no real robotic arm?

items.answer: There was no real robot then, no real robotic arm to do this for us. So there were two solutions. One was to put it into 3D animation, where you can do whatever you want. The other was to make a simple robot system, but since there was no robotic arm, we simply made the cup into a robot: we fabricated a large cup-like object with a motor underneath, so the cup could autonomously drive on a tabletop. items.question: Why did you find your initial research in Stanford's electrical engineering department a poor fit for you?

items.answer: I quickly found that I was not suited to it or did not like it. Why? When I had previously done device physics, I first used mathematics and physics to model something. items.question: How did your experience with semiconductor fabrication at Stanford shape your decision to switch to AI?
items.object: The decision to leave semiconductor research at Stanford and switch to AI
items.answer:
It is a kind of black box, so you have to experiment. When I got to Stanford, Stanford EE had me enter the clean room and said: do not build mathematical models anymore, just try things. That was very different from my personal habits of thought. You can think of an idea quickly, but it takes a month to complete the entire fabrication process for a chip and then measure its electrical properties. So you think quickly but work very slowly. Very slowly. The verification time is extremely long. And you cannot control it. And my hands are clumsy.

For example, I would drop a chip in hydrofluoric acid. It needed to etch for fifteen seconds, but Stanford was unbelievably primitive—you may think semiconductor fabs are fully automated and extremely advanced. In fact, for PhD students, even hydrofluoric acid can kill you if enough enters your body, with no cure. items.question: Why did you see category-level object pose estimation as a meaningful extension of existing work in robot vision?
items.object: Category-level object pose estimation
items.answer:
In the first project, we estimated object states, and at the time I felt that such states—whether a bottle is open, whether it has a cap, whether it is open or closed—were too coarse. Could we describe an object’s state more precisely? That precise description is its three-dimensional position and three-dimensional rotation. In robot vision, that is called an object’s six-dimensional pose, or 6D pose.

If we made it precise with 6D pose, we found that everyone else’s 6D pose work was for a single object: you define where that object’s coordinate origin is, and where its X, Y, and Z axes are. Now you have defined the object’s origin and canonical orientation. Then, if the object is lying here, tell me its relative rotation and translation from that original coordinate system. Before my work, this was called instance-level object pose estimation: you had to give me the specific object instance and its original definition. Only then could I tell you how much it had rotated and translated relative to your original definition. That sounds reasonable, but as I said in the previous work about picking up a cup, I don’t actually care what particular cup it is. But now you are saying that, in order to know its 6D pose, I need to build a digital model for every cup, label where its origin is, and label which way is up. Humans definitely do not understand object states that way.

For objects of the same category, we can clearly say that, regardless of the patterns printed on them, these mugs are lined up with their openings facing up and their handles facing right. Then I do not need labels for an object’s origin and X-axis; I can directly discuss the pose of an unseen instance within that object category.

items.question: How did you approach the lack of training data for category-level object pose estimation?
items.object: Mixed-reality synthetic data for category-level object pose estimation
items.answer:
For a mug, the traditional approach is to scan a model of every mug, put that model into environments and photograph it extensively, yielding images labeled with the mug’s 6D pose; then you predict the 6D pose from a new image. But at the category level, there might be infinitely many mugs. You cannot photograph every mug, label its 6D pose, build a training set covering all mugs, and then learn to generalize to any new mug. The real data does not exist. You cannot crawl every mug on the Internet and label its 6D pose. And as a PhD student working alone—this was a single-first-author paper—I could not even photograph and label enough myself.

So we used graphics: we rendered many digital mug assets into real environments and created a mixed-reality dataset. Specifically, because we focused on tabletop scenes, I took a camera to an IKEA in the Bay Area. I told them I was doing research and needed tabletop scenes; they said to take as many photos as I wanted, with no copyright issue. I took an RGB-D camera into IKEA, where there were many tables, beds, and all kinds of flat surfaces. I photographed RGB and corresponding depth, extracted the tabletop from the depth, placed a digital mug exactly on the tabletop, and rendered it into the foreground of the IKEA background. So the background was real and the foreground was fake. From a distance, it looked quite real. Since it was rendered, we knew exactly how it was placed in the graphics interface—its ground truth pose was labeled automatically. This produced a dataset of hundreds of thousands of images to train category-level object pose estimation.

So at the time, I opened up a direction: generalizably predicting the poses of objects from known categories. But there was no data. We mixed real backgrounds with virtual foregrounds to form what we called mixed-reality data, then trained with sim-to-real, or mix-to-real, and tested in the real world. That is what you use today. Of course, today’s technology has gone through many iterations, but the source of that idea was my second project. I started it around early 2018; it became a CVPR 2019 oral. After I published that first paper, by 2021 I had essentially created a subfield within CVPR submissions. It was very interesting. And many people kept competing on the benchmark for my paper. My original dataset, including its synthetic data, became a dataset people repeatedly benchmarked against.

It was an extension of a classic problem in robot vision. Pose estimation has a long history in robot vision, but people generally studied known objects. They had not reached the point where, given an object and knowing only its category, one could estimate its pose. So it was a conceptual extension, and technically we used synthetic data for the task. We did not collect data at massive scale, but it still had some effect in the real world.

items.question: How do you see your early research as connected to the core problems of embodied intelligence?
items.object: The connection between He Wang’s early research and embodied intelligence
items.answer: The core of embodied intelligence is the perception-action loop: you have to be proactive. items.question: How do you understand the surge of enthusiasm for embodied AI after Google’s PaLM-E appeared?
items.object: Google’s PaLM-E and the growing enthusiasm for embodied AI
items.answer: The way I see it, intelligent robots, or embodied AI: at first, people had imagination about it, but it was not so hot because it felt as though, to do one thing, you needed data, and after learning from that data you could only solve that one capability—doing that one job. It did not sound as if it had the potential to become general all at once. Or, for embodied intelligence, every physical task requires collecting data before you can do that one thing, so the marginal cost does not fall. In the end, it is a method, but it cannot become a revolutionary technology. But Google’s PaLM-E called itself an embodied multimodal large model. By today’s strict standards, it is not even embodied, because it does not output actions at all; essentially it is an agent that calls smaller models to execute actions. But after that work came out, people said, wow, a large language model can be the brain, a Turing-style large model can be the brain, commanding smaller models that do work; then it can carry out open instructions—say anything and it does it. That sounded like a paradigm for a general robot. If it could become general, the potential of robots would be enormous. A home is one environment that requires generality. If you could make home robots, each robot would have more value than a car, but volumes larger than smartphones. More expensive than a car, with greater volume than smartphones. If such a thing could be built, would it not become the world’s number-one industry? So suddenly everyone felt they had to do it and invest in it. ChatGPT came out at the end of 2022, and PaLM-E came out in early 2023.

items.question: How did you assess whether you were ready to found an embodied intelligence company in early 2023?

items.answer: My biggest problem was that I had not done hardware myself before. The hardware on the market that I had used—after setting up the Embodied Intelligence Center at Zhiyuan Institute, we immediately used hardware from several companies, which I will not name; some have now gone bankrupt—was all no good. We wanted to build intelligence for it and found the hardware was terrible. Never mind intelligence; it could not even execute. These were wheeled or legged machines moving around and working in the real world. Machines with hands. It was impossible. I said: you want me to found a company, but all current market hardware is junk, and I do not make hardware myself—so what would the company rely on for the hardware body? At that point he was not necessarily trying to persuade me to start a company; he also wanted to discuss whether this was viable and what it could do. My view then was that someone had to fill all the gaps I had just described before we could start a company together. Later, we joined forces with the Galbot team.

items.question: Why do you see Galbot’s choice of wheeled robot hardware as pragmatic?
items.object: Galbot’s pragmatic hardware strategy for commercial robots
items.answer:
Fundamentally, I think you must have a first step. If in that first step you challenge extremely immature hardware technologies that have never been mass-produced, you are in fact dragging down your intelligence. Relatively mature—nothing in mechanical technology today is fully mature, I can tell you—means that unless something has reached hundreds of thousands, preferably millions, in production volume, it has not truly undergone mass production. Cars: this industry is more than a hundred years old, yet when a new model comes out today, it still has all kinds of problems people see. Yield rates, reliability, and aspects people find unsatisfactory. And robots—especially humanoid robots—have never been mass-produced at any point in history. Many upstream parts of our supply chain have not been mass-produced either. In that situation, if you choose components that have gone through production of more than ten thousand units, you can count that as small- to medium-scale mass production. It is relatively more reliable, because such a large robot body has N components; if any one fails, the robot fails. If you choose an aggressive solution now, then for quite some time you will encounter products that do not work after shipment, long iteration cycles, and ultimately a drag on your commercialization pace.

And in doing work, do not add unreliable or unnecessary parts unless necessary—is that not the logic? The customer you deliver to is different from a consumer-facing application. items.question: How do you understand the difference between the physical intelligent agents you are developing and older industrial robots equipped with 3D vision?

items.answer: Data-driven systems in the past, combined with industrial robot arms, mainly used some 3D vision for localization. items.question: How do you decide which physical manipulation skills to develop for a commercially viable robot?

items.question: Why do you see generalization as essential to the business model of an embodied-intelligence company?
items.object: Generalization and commercial scalability in embodied-intelligence companies
items.answer: The economics do not add up otherwise. But when moving to the next scenario, the entire solution must be redone from scratch. The marginal cost does not fall at all. That is a very common situation in industrial vision. Different manufacturers have different materials. For these different materials and shapes, I need to remodel and create templates, and so on. Every project requires a constant investment of labor, R&D, and delivery time. In that case, with unlimited people it could be done at scale, but it is not replicable. After I get a solution for one manufacturer, I switch to another and find I have to develop it all over again. Then your scale can only reach so far. Reaching revenue of a few hundred million would already be remarkable, because frankly the company does not make money—it is all labor-intensive work. That too is a proven business model. For our generation of embodied-intelligence companies, if we fall into either model, our ultimate ceiling cannot exceed them. We cannot have the kind of capital support the United States has, where a company can exist for decades without making a profit. items.question: Why do you reject the claim that robot skills learned from synthetic data cannot transfer to the real world?
items.object: Misconceptions about transferring robot skills learned from synthetic data to the real world
items.answer:
There are several misconceptions about synthetic data. The first is that synthetic data’s physics are entirely different from the real world. Well, not entirely different—just not exactly the same. In physical simulation, numerical methods can only approximate, or the formulas themselves are not exactly consistent with the most precise real-world physics; they approximate real physical phenomena. So people say sim-to-real is impossible. First, that has already been completely disproven. Why are all humanoid-robot skills for walking, jumping, and running today obtained through sim-to-real, using large-scale reinforcement learning in simulators? So if someone says sim-to-real does not work, they must answer why Unitree’s sim-to-real works.

Why do people still say it does not work? They say Unitree’s sim-to-real involves only the body, legs, feet, and contact with the ground, without vision. It is sim-to-real based on kinematic and dynamic state variables. But once you add vision, the rendered images differ from the real world, so they say sim-to-real cannot work after adding the visual modality. If you think carefully, that too is entirely wrong. First, even in the small-model era, we demonstrated through a series of physically rendered and physically simulated experiments that objects such as transparent broken glass shards can be learned entirely from synthetic data for how to grasp them, and can transfer sim-to-real in the real world. In 2023, this was the first method introduced globally that generalized fully across materials for grasping. In the small-model era, I could already close the visual sim-to-real gap.

In the VLA large-model era, this has become even more certain. Why? Because the foundation of VLA is VLM, and VLM training data is not only real data. It also includes huge amounts of animation and movie data, which mix real and fake. Can a VLM that understands the real world not understand the plot when it sees Donald Duck and Mickey Mouse?

items.answer: I think it needs to understand how operating this object may produce certain dynamics—the physical process. Texture and material are not things that VLMs, and VLAs derived from VLM large models, cannot transfer across. In the large-model era, this visual gap is even less of a gap. At most, there is a physical gap. Why can humanoid-robot walking be handled relatively well now? Whether the ground becomes steel or sand, the physical process is relatively just a foot contacting the ground and receiving a support force. Manipulation, however, involves threading a needle, folding clothes, grasping soft objects, grasping fragile objects, and all kinds of things. For some physical processes, current simulation produces only a small gap. For others, a certain gap still exists. Our view is that for moving, picking, and placing, we can make that gap small enough using current simulation technology. So we have demonstrated everything from grasping to dexterous-hand manipulation, and then flexible objects, folding clothes, and hanging clothes. We generated large amounts of synthetic data through physical synthesis and simulation, and it can all transfer to the real world. For things I cannot do now, I admit there are things I cannot do, such as tying shoelaces. This simulation process involves multipoint, multisurface, flexible, compressible contact, and it really cannot yet be simulated very realistically. items.question: What do you consider a real product in the embodied-intelligence industry?
items.object: Productivity as the standard for embodied-intelligence products
items.answer: I think it must be able to generate productivity—generate a solution—but it does not necessarily have to be a complete solution. At the current stage, you can have, for example, one area of a room where the robot can do the work, and another area where it cannot, with people covering the gap. So a complete solution is not necessarily required. Although our current 24-hour pharmacies aim to provide a complete solution—that is harder—we can also take a step back and have human-machine collaboration. So I think productivity is a solution. What is productivity? It means that, per unit of time, the work you do must be comparable to that of a person. The high-quality, new-quality productivity you create today is the real product of this industry. items.question: Why do you see the development of humanoid-robot productivity as especially important for China?
items.object: Humanoid-robot productivity as a response to China’s aging population and labor shortage
items.answer: What we are looking at today is extremely important for China. Because China’s aging population and declining birthrate mean that every five years, our labor force—the available labor force—drops by some fraction of a percentage point. Ten or twenty years from now, our labor force may be less than half what it is today. But our elderly population will be much larger than it is today. Under these circumstances, if we do not rapidly advance the development of humanoid-robot productivity, China’s manufacturing industry will face an enormous labor shortage, and the service sector will be the same. Look at Japan: it was originally a non-immigration country that did not accept people without Japanese nationality, but now, because its labor shortage is so severe, it accepts everything. Yet the labor shortage is still especially severe. I went to Japan to investigate, and Japanese people told me that now, once young people graduate, everyone has a job, and the benefits are especially good. As soon as you ask them to work overtime, they leave—they resign directly. They can immediately find another job. Every industry lacks people, and I was told that every age group lacks people. This is the social reality of Japan after it entered deep aging. But Japan has a smaller population base, and neighboring countries such as China, Vietnam, and Cambodia can help fill the gap, so its society is still in a stage where it can function. What about China? If we are short 100 million workers, who in the world can provide us with 100 million workers? We can foresee that in the future aging society, China will face a predicament even more difficult than Japan’s.

items.question: How do you understand Galbot’s responsibility to prevent humanoid robotics from becoming a bubble?
items.object: Galbot’s responsibility to prevent a humanoid-robotics bubble
items.answer: What I see as Galbot’s responsibility is that this absolutely must not become a bubble. Once it is falsified—or considered to fall short of expectations—it may cause the entire industry to enter an ice age. And then, for China’s future development, it would mean that no solution path could be put forward. This is what we are emphasizing especially now. Do not do things that damage our industry’s reputation—for example, promising people that once they collect data, they can train it; that once they build a factory, they can have skills; that I sell you robots, you collect data, you train them, and tomorrow they are your employees. These models are very frightening. They are smashing this industry’s rice bowl. If someone smashes it this way, I worry whether the industry will see some negative—rather negative—news that affects the situation of the leading companies like us that want to get things done, have a sense of purpose, and truly have responsibility.

items.question: How do you understand NVIDIA’s strong commitment to synthetic data for embodied intelligence?
items.object: NVIDIA’s commitment to synthetic data for embodied intelligence
items.answer: My understanding is that NVIDIA, besides Galbot, is a major company worldwide that strongly follows the synthetic-data technical route. Their reasoning is even simpler: they believe that having GPUs should solve every problem. If problems other than GPUs are also needed, then they cannot advance it as quickly. Synthetic data means using GPUs for rendering and simulation, then using more advanced GPUs for computation. So NVIDIA strongly agrees that if synthetic data can be made to work, then NVIDIA can support half the sky of embodied intelligence. So Jensen Huang invited me because he wanted to hear how we were doing with synthetic data. I also opened my phone and showed him the level we had reached with a series of work done entirely with synthetic data.

items.question: How do you assess the prospect of embodied intelligence reaching maturity within one or two years?
items.object: The prospects for embodied intelligence reaching maturity
items.answer: Our understanding of central control nerves—the entire humanoid-robotics field’s understanding of biomimetic, human-like central motor-control nerves—is still very primitive. A lot of the knowledge runs counter to our first intuition. For example, the cerebellum actually has more neurons than the cerebrum. For example, movement generation actually relies on the cerebrum, while the cerebellum performs a series of controls. I can only say that, in human embodied manipulation and whole-body control, there are very, very many secrets in human biomimetic—human-like—central control nerves. At present, whether using VR or using large models over small models and so on, we have not completely found a way to achieve them. So my overall view of embodied intelligence is that it still has room for continuous exploration over decades. Rather than having a moment of great maturity and complete fulfillment appear in one or two years—that is impossible.

items.question: Why would you recommend A Brief History of Time as a must-read book?
items.object: A Brief History of Time
items.answer: The first I would recommend is A Brief History of Time. It was a book I read in middle school, but I continued rereading it in high school and college. The laws behind nature and physics are just so wonderful. Even today, we have not exhausted what all the most fundamental laws of the material world are. I think that as I repeatedly read this book and sought to understand the laws behind space and time, I developed a way of thinking centered on exploring the laws and essence of how things develop. So many terms we use today, including in business, such as thinking from first principles—where do first principles come from? In physics, this is called ab initio computation, first-principles computation. So learning physics well, and understanding the most essential thinking in physics, can greatly improve a person’s level of thought and ability to think. Of course, learning physics well cannot rely on A Brief History of Time alone. It is simply a very fascinating popular-science physics book; it may not even explain things that clearly, but it lets you understand how profound they are.

items.answer: I would combine them. They each have their own imperfections. As Cao Cao went along, whether his original aspiration was really for the Han dynasty changed in the end. Yet he was still very restrained: he would rather be King Wen of Zhou than usurp the throne while he was alive. Zhuge Liang’s greatest issue was that he persisted with his idealism to the end, but the resources he could mobilize and the things he could change were far too limited. If he could have had better strategic planning like Cao Cao, and gathered resources into his hands earlier. At the same time, like Zhuge Liang, maintain one’s original heart. Liu Bei was gone, yet he would absolutely never covet Liu Shan’s position. Combining these two points better matches our dream of doing humanoid robotics today. In the end, this undertaking will certainly bring benefits to humanity. Once this undertaking succeeds, it will certainly become a pillar at the national level, dedicated to the nation and dedicated to the world. This is why I say Cao Cao and Zhuge Liang are both indispensable. If something like productivity ultimately becomes purely about competing with us for jobs and taking everyone’s jobs, then it cannot last. And the whole world will oppose it. Therefore, our original aspiration is to serve the people. Even after this grows large, we must ultimately ensure that society can develop healthily.

items.object: The time pressure of pursuing high academic publication volume
items.answer: I think if you are a pure scholar, and you think about publishing dozens of CVPR papers and dozens of ICC papers this year, then you will always feel you do not have enough time.
quotes: If you are a pure scholar, and you think about publishing dozens of CVPR papers and dozens of ICC papers this year, then you will always feel you do not have enough time.

rubrics.text: The response states that a pure scholar aiming to publish dozens of CVPR papers and dozens of ICC papers in a year will continually feel that there is not enough time.
